nodes.label: Agglutination / Suffix Stacking
nodes.rationale: Multiple suffixes (plural, possessive, case) stack on one noun stem, each contributing one independently identifiable piece of meaning, because Hungarian grammar is agglutinative rather than fusional; case sits outermost because it operates on the already fully-inflected word form, not the bare root.

nodes.label: The Hungarian Case System (23 cases)
nodes.rationale: Hungarian expresses grammatical relations through an extensive suffixal case system rather than prepositions because case marking is handled by the same agglutinative suffixation as everything else in the language; cases sit outermost (after plural/possessive suffixes) because they operate on the whole inflected word, and vowel harmony governs which allomorph surfaces for the same reason it governs plural/possessive suffix choice.

nodes.label: Inessive Case (-ban/-ben)
nodes.rationale: Inessive is treated as the paradigm representative for 'other locative cases' because nearly every non-superessive locative case suffixes identically to it - only the superessive requires a different, always-linking-vowel pattern - so explaining inessive's suffixation rules economically explains most of the locative group at once.

nodes.label: Locative Cases Group (interior/exterior/near x motion-toward/static/motion-away)
nodes.rationale: Hungarian locative cases are organized along interior/exterior/near axes crossed with motion-toward/static/motion-away, giving a systematic grid because spatial relations are decomposed into these independent parameters rather than lexicalized case-by-case, letting one suffix pattern generalize across many concrete spatial meanings.

nodes.label: Oblique Cases Group (dative, instrumental, translative, causal-final, essive-formal, terminative, distributive, essive)
nodes.rationale: Oblique cases are grouped as 'everything else' because they don't fit the locative spatial grid or the two grammatical cases; several originated as extensions of spatial/directional meaning into abstract domains (e.g. translative 'into' extended to 'becoming'), which is why more than one shows v-initial assimilation inherited from a shared historical source.
nodes.norm_label: oblique cases group (dative, instrumental, translative, causal-final, essive-formal, terminative, distributive, essive)

nodes.label: v-Assimilation of Instrumental (-val/-vel) and Translative (-va/-ve) Suffixes
nodes.rationale: The instrumental and translative suffixes' initial v regressively assimilates to the stem's final consonant (baratommal, lannyal, vizze, borra) because Hungarian resolves consonant-final-stem plus v-initial-suffix clusters by full place assimilation rather than by inserting a linking vowel, marking these two cases as a distinct 'v-assimilating' family.
nodes.norm_label: v-assimilation of instrumental (-val/-vel) and translative (-va/-ve) suffixes

nodes.label: Verb/Case Government
nodes.rationale: A single Hungarian verb can take different case-marked complements for systematically different meanings (Hiszek Janosban 'I believe in Janos' vs Hiszek Janosnak 'I believe Janos') because case substitutes for what English does with distinct prepositions or verbs - the case itself carries part of the semantic distinction, which is why a dictionary must list a verb's governed case alongside its meaning.

nodes.label: Hungarian Article System (definite/indefinite/zero)
nodes.rationale: Hungarian requires the definite article in more environments than English (possessed nouns, possessive pronouns, demonstratives, many abstracts, generic reference) because the article's function has broadened beyond marking specific reference alone; it never inflects for case/number because it is not part of the noun's own agglutinative suffix chain.

nodes.label: Hungarian Noun Stem Classes (vowel-final, low-vowel, v-stem, -alom/-elem, fleeting-vowel, regular)
nodes.rationale: Hungarian classifies nouns by how their stem behaves under suffixation because the bare nominative-singular citation form often hides the 'real' stem (e.g. lo vs lov-); the alternation is only revealed once a suffix, canonically the plural, is attached, so class membership has to be memorized rather than predicted from the singular alone.
nodes.norm_label: hungarian noun stem classes (vowel-final, low-vowel, v-stem, -alom/-elem, fleeting-vowel, regular)

nodes.label: Singular/Plural Usage Rules Beyond Count
nodes.rationale: Hungarian uses the singular where English uses the plural (after numerals, for naturally-paired body parts/accessories, for generic reference) because in each case the noun denotes a category or a counted unit rather than a set of discrete countable individuals - the numeral already carries plurality, and paired items are conceived of as one type-referent.

nodes.label: Consonant Length (Gemination)
nodes.rationale: Consonant length is phonemic in Hungarian (szeretem 'I love' vs szerettem 'I loved' differ only by length) because it functions as a genuine segmental contrast rather than an allophonic detail, so morphological processes producing long consonants are treated as meaningful outputs, not spelling quirks.

nodes.label: Consonant Lengthening Before j
nodes.rationale: d/gy/t/ty/n/ny lengthen rather than surface as clusters before a j-initial suffix because Hungarian resolves these obstruent+j sequences via regressive place assimilation into one long palatal consonant; l instead fully assimilates to long jj, which is why Rounds flags it as the one deviation within the same rule.

nodes.label: Assimilation of Sibilants
nodes.rationale: Hissing sibilants (sz, z) become hushing (s/zs-like) before a hushing sibilant because sibilant place-of-articulation assimilates regressively just as voicing does, producing a long hushing consonant; ordinary voicing/devoicing rules still apply on top since the two processes act on different features simultaneously.

nodes.label: Hungarian Stress and Intonation Rules
nodes.rationale: Word-initial stress is fixed and grammatically inert in Hungarian, so intonation rather than stress placement carries sentence-level distinctions - a rise-fall pitch pattern, not a stress shift, is the primary (sometimes only) signal distinguishing a declarative from a yes/no question reading of an otherwise identical sentence.

nodes.label: Voicing and Devoicing Assimilation
nodes.rationale: Hungarian obstruents assimilate in voicing to whichever consonant follows across a morpheme/word boundary because voicing agreement is enforced regressively; v never triggers voicing (though it can itself devoice) and h has no voiced counterpart, which is why those two consonants sit outside the normal voiced/unvoiced pairing.

nodes.label: Neutral Vowels in Vowel Harmony
nodes.rationale: Front unrounded vowels (i, i, e, e-acute) carry no inherent front/back marking and co-occur with either class, so a mixed back+neutral stem defaults to back and an all-neutral stem defaults to front (with lexically memorized exceptions, e.g. verb root sziv 'inhale') because neutral vowels alone give the harmony system no positive evidence for a suffix variant.

nodes.label: Vowel Harmony
nodes.rationale: Suffixes carry front/back (and rounded/unrounded) vowel allomorphs because Hungarian requires front-or-back vowel assonance to be maintained across an entire native word; the suffix's vowel changes shape to agree with the stem's own vowel class rather than the reverse, which is why case, plural, and possessive paradigms each have 2-3 allomorphs.
